full_judgment:
2. In Writ Petition No. 201 of 1996, Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned orders dated 14-1-1996 as endorsed in 17 Bills of Entry vide Annexures- V to V -16 pursuant to impugned Notification being SRO No. 215-Ain/951644/Shulko dated 12-12-95 video  Annexure-U refusing to assess customs duties on the  goods imported by the petitioner on the basis of  Clean Report of Finding (CRF) value vide Annexure- T pursuant to SRO No. 316-Ain/94  /1568/Shulko dated 3-11-94 vide Annexure-A should not be declared to be without lawful authority and  are of no legal effect. Pending hearing of the Rule, the respondents were directed to allow the petitioner to release the reconditioned cars on the basis of payment of duty on CRF value of the goods. 

 3. In Writ Petition No. 2035 of 1996, Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned orders dated 6-6-96 vide Annexures-B Series should not be declared to void and without lawful authority and are of no legal effect and as to why the Respondents should not  directed to levy and collect customs duty, VAT and  other charges in respect of the said imported  consignments on the basis of R&F value as declared  by the petitioner. In this case also, pending hearing of the Rule, the respondents were directed to allow the petitioner to release the goods on payment of the duties on the cost and freight (C&F) value. 

 4. In Writ Petition No. 201 of 1996, the petitioner stated that he is the sole proprietor of MIs Rising Traders of OR Nizam Road, Chittagong. In pursuance of Notification being SRO No. 316-Ain/94/1568/Sulko dated 3-11-1994, which was published in the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary on 5-11-1994, the customs duties were required to be assessed on the imported reconditioned cars on the basis of Clean Report of Finding (CRF as to their quality, quantity and value issued by an approved pre-Shipment Inspection Agent, in short, PSI Agent, enlisted at Appendix-l of the said SRO. The aforesaid SRO dated 3-11-1994 issued under section 25A of the Customs Act 1969 specifically provides that in the event of the Commissioner of Customs failing to approve the CRF, he may refer the matter to the National Board of Revenue, but must in the meantime allow provisional assessment and release of the goods on payment of customs duties on the basis of the value certified by the CRF. The petitioner opened letter of credit on 8-11-95 valued US dollar 32,800 at C&F, Chittagong, issued by the National Credit and Commerce Bank Limited, Khatunganj Branch, Chittagong, for import from Japan of a consignment of 17 units of used vehicles which is peculiarly known as re-conditioned vehicles in accordance with the pro forma invoice dated 1-11-95. The goods were duly shipped/rom Japan under a set of 17 commercial invoices dated 22-11-95 with related bills of lading dated 28-11-95. Prior to the shipment, the goods were duly inspected on 22-11-95 by Bureau Veritas, a duly enlisted PSI Agent, who issued CRF on 11-12-95 in respect of quality, quantity, price and NS Code thereof in compliance with the said SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-94 issued under section 25A of the Customs Act. 

 5. After letter of credit had been opened and the said goods were shipped from Japan, the respondent No. 4 issued a Notification being SRO No. 215-Ain/95/1644/Shulko dated 12-12-95 (which is the impugned notification) which purported to amend SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-94 by excluding from its  ambit 12 kinds of goods including car/micro- bus/jeep/pick-ups classified under HS Code No. 87'03 and directing that CRF issued by PSI Agent would not be applicable in respect of such goods. The goods of the petitioner arrived at Chittagong Port on 23-12-95 on the vessel Morning Bright and then the petitioner submitted the shipping documents including the bills of entry and CRF to the Customs Authority through his Clearing and Forwarding Agent on 13-1-96 in order to take delivery of goods on payment of customs duties, V AT and other charges thereon on the basis of the CRF value. The petitioner thereafter came to learn that respondent No.2 has issued 17 impugned orders all dated 14-1-96 pursuant-to SRO No. 215 dated 12-12-95 refusing to allow the petitioners to clear the goods on payment of customs duties on the basis  CRF value and directing that the goods be  examined for the purpose of assessment of customs duties and other charges thereon instead of assessing the same on the basis of the invoice value as certified in the CRF pursuant to SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-94. The respondent No. 1 failed to assess customs duties on the goods on the basis of CRF value and to release the same on payment of customs duties by the petitioner pursuant to SRO No: 316 dated 31-11-94. The petitioner then came to learn that respondent No. 2 had directed to assess the duties and taxes on the basis of 'Yellow Book' value instead of CRF value. 

 6. It is submitted by the petitioner that the respondents are bound to release the goods on realising the duties on the basis of CRF value in pursuance of SRO No. 316 dated 3•11•94. It is further submitted that the very subsequent SRO No. 215 dated 1'2•12•95 is bad in law in view of the fact that the said amended SRO 215 is ultra vires section 25A of the Customs Act. It is further submitted that in respect of the goods of the present petitioner the SRO No. 215 dated 12•12-95 has no manner of application. This imposition of duties on Yellow Book value is absolutely without jurisdiction in view of the fact that this Yellow Book value has no legal sanction. The petitioner has also taken the ground that the actions of the respondents are violative of the provisions of Articles 27, 31, 40, 42 and 83 of the Constitution. 

 7. The respondent Nos. 4 and 5 have filed affidavit-in-opposition and they also filed a supplementary affidavit-in-opposition in this case. In this affidavit-in-opposition the respondents have denied the allegations made by the petitioner in the writ petition. It is their case that in the instant case the duty should be assessed on the Yellow Book value inasmuch as this importation of used cars is out of the ambit of the CRF value. It is their case that there is no illegality in assessing the duties on the basis of Yellow' Book value. By the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition the respondents have annexed several papers and documents in order to show that the customs authority is entitled to assess customs duty on the basis of Yellow Book value. The petitioner also filed an affidavit-in-reply and a supplementary affidavit-in-reply stating that this Yellow Book value has got no legal sanction and, as such, this imposition of the duties upon the petitioner's goods is violative of the provisions of section 25A of the Customs Act. 

 9. Dr Kamal Hossain and Mr AF Hasan Arif, the learned Advocates, appeared for the petitioner in this case. They submit that the Notification vide SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-94 was issued under section 25A of the Customs Act and in that Notification, 14 terms and conditions have been incorporated. In that Notification the Appendix-I shows 5 recognised PSI Agents one of whom was Bureau Veritas. The impugned Notification vide SRO No. 215 dated 12-12-95 shows that the appendix No.2 was amended by which the 12 kinds of goods were brought out from the ambit of Notification vide SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-94. It shows that vide this impugned Notification dated 12-12-95 issued under section 25A of the .Customs Act simply these 12 kinds of goods were taken out from imposition of duties on the basis of CRF value. The learned Advocate submits that this Notification is repugnant to section 25A of the Customs Act and the earlier Notification dated 3-11-94. 

 10. Section 25A of the Customs Act as stood on 30th June, 1955, runs as follows: "25A. Assessment on the basis of certificate issued by pre-shipment inspection agencies: Notwithstanding anything contained in any other section of this Act, the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, declare that the quality, quantity, price and customs classification of goods verified and certified in the prescribed manner by an approved pre-shipment inspection agency will be accepted as the basis of assessment. Explanation-For the purpose of this section, "price" shall mean the normal price and (2) of section 25." The SRO 316 dated 3.11.94 was issued by the authority in pursuance of section 25A of the Customs Act. The amendment of the aforesaid SRO was also made by the self-same authority vide SRO No. 215 dated 12•12•95 in pursuance of the this amended SRO dated 12•12•95 authority only provisions of section 25A of the Customs Act. By amended the Appendix•2 and by that amendment provision was made to the effect that the 12 kinds of goods when the same will be imported, will not be subject to payment of customs duties on the basis of CRF value. So, the authority which issued the SRO dated 3•11•94 also amended the aforesaid SRO vide issuing another SRO No. 215 dated 12•12•95 under section 25A of the said Act. As such, we do not find any reason as to why this amended Notification dated 12•12•95 should be called ultra vires section 25A of 

 11. The learned Advocates for the petitioner submit that when the letters of credit were opened on 8•11•95, invoices were issued on 22•11•95, bills of lading were issued on 28•11•95 and CRF was granted on 11•12•95, the previous SRO dated 3•11•94 was in force. As soon as the CRF was granted on 11•12•95 the vested right was created in favour of the petitioner to get the goods released on payment of duties on the CRF value. They submit that since the amendment was made vide SRO dated 12•12•95, the same will not be applicable in the case of the petitioner in view of the fact that the CRF was granted on 11•12•95 which was one day earlier of the amended Notification dated 12•12•95. Since before the subsequent Notification dated 12•12•95 came into force, the right of the petitioner was accrued on 11•12•95 and, as such, this amended Notification dated 12•12•95 has no manner of application in the case of the petitioner. 

 12. The learned Advocate for the petitioner further submits that section 2SA of the Customs Act will have independent application in view of the fact that non-obstante clause has been added• in that section itself. Since the provisions of section 2SA are completely and independently applicable in the matter of importing goods as covered under CRF, there is no option of the authority but to release the goods on imposing duty upon the CRF value. Since in the instant case by Gazette notification the PSI Agent has been appointed and upto the date of the  certificate granted by PSI Agent, the SRO No.315  dated 3•11•94 was in force, and as such, the respondents are under legal obligation to release the goods on the basis of imposition of duty upon CRF value. 

 14. Two writ petitions, namely, Writ Petition No. 4337 of 1996 and Writ Petition No. 4336 of 1996 were heard and disposed of by this Bench on 17 -12-96 wherein this Court discharged the aforesaid two Rules. In that Judgment, this Court discussed different provisions of the Customs Act as well as some authorities and held that the price of the goods, prevailing or in force at the time of submission of bill of entry to the authority will be the basis for imposition of customs duty for the goods. In the instant case we also hold that the section 25A with explanation shall be read along with sections 25, 30 and 30A of the Customs Act and the customs duty will be imposed upon the value of the goods prevailing or in force at the time when the bill of entry along will other papers will be submitted to the authorities. Since in the instant case the bills of entry were submitted to the authority for clearance of the goods on 13-1-96, the petitioner shall have to pay the customs duties on the basis of the price of the goods fixed by the authority then prevailing that is on 13-1-96. 

 15. Dr Kamal Hossain submits that CRF was granted on 11-12-95 and on that day the right of the present petitioner was accrued to get the goods released on paying customs duty on the basis of CRF value. It is difficult for us to accept the above contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner. 

 16. In support of the contentions that the importer will have to pay the duties on the value of the goods at the rate prevailing on the date of submission of bill of entry, the learned Advocate for the respondents have referred to several decisions in the cases of Glaxo Laboratories vs. A V Venkateswaran, AIR 1959 (Born) 372, Sharaf Faridi vs. Federation of Pakistan, PLD 1989 (Kar) 457, 621, Shah Devchand vs. Union of India, AIR 1991 (SC) 1931,764, Ramkrishna Theatres Ltd. vs. GI & C Corporation, AIR 1993 (Kerala) TC 98, Bharat Surfactant (Pv.) Ltd vs. Union of India, AIR 1989 (SC) 2059), Afgan Commercial Co vs. Union of India, AIR 1953 (Punj) 225, Public Prosecutor vs. Venkata Reddy, AIR 1961 (Andaw) 107, Kuwait Flour Mills Co vs. MV Kashmir, PW 1989 (Har) 60 end Assistant Controller of Customs and 3 others vs. Messrs Link Engineering Company Ltd. 1989 SCMR 1698. In our recent judgment this Bench also held the similar view following other decisions to the effect that the importers are liable to pay customs duties on the basis of the value of the goods which is in force on the day when the bill of entry is produced before the authority. So, we do not find any substance in the submissions of the learned Advocates for the petitioner. 

 17. In the Writ application at paragraph 12 it is stated by the petitioner that the authorities arbitrarily directed to pay the customs duties on the basis of Yellow Book value instead of CRF value. In reply to the statement made in paragraph 12 of the writ petition, it is stated by the Respondent Nos. 4 in paragraph 10 of the affidavit-in-opposition that the customs duties 0:1 the imported cars was not assessed on the basis of CRF value because the CRF had already been withdrawn from the imported goods in question by SRO dated 12-12-95 and respondent No.2 had correctly and lawfully directed to assess the duties and taxes on the basis of Yellow Book value. It is further stated that this Yellow Book value has a basis and standard having authentic value of the goods in question as determined by the manufacturers' Association of Japan, a semi- government organization, with high credibility and standard in the country as well as other importing countries. When the bill of entry was submitted in the instant case on 13-1-96 the importer is required to pay the customs duty on the basis of the Yellow Book value which was in force at that time. 

 18. The learned Advocates for the petitioner have vehemently challenged the imposition of the duties on the basis of Yellow Book value. It is their case that this Yellow Book has no legal sanction. It is neither a rule nor any notification nor any regulation under any authority of law of this country. Since this Yellow Book is neither any Act nor any Ordinance nor any Rule nor any Regulation in any manner whatsoever, imposition of the duties on the basis of such Yellow Book is absolutely illegal and without jurisdiction. Not only that, it offends Article 83 of the Constitution. It is further submitted that without passing any law by the Parliament or by any other delegated authority, no Rule or Regulation can be made for imposition of duties and taxes upon any person. As such, this Yellow Book value has no legal basis. 

 19. The learned Advocates for the respondents have produced before us a booklet named 'Yellow Book' from which they wanted to show the price of cars which were given by the manufacturers of different companies with regard to different kinds of motor vehicles manufactured in Japan. It is the case of the Respondents that the dishonest business people of the country with malafide intention to deprive the Government of having actual customs duties, in connivance with the foreign exporters and corrupt officers used to show the lesser value of the goods in their invoices so that they are required to pay customs duties in Bangladesh at a lesser rate. In order to stop this corrupt practice of these unscrupulous businessmen and also for the interest of the country, Government brought this booklet from Japan, namely, Yellow Book wherein the HS Codes of different cars with the prices have been incorporated. The authority, on the basis of such price of the different imported goods shown by the manufacturers in the Yellow Book used to impose the customs duties here, although in the invoices, the importers used to show the lesser price of the imported goods. In such a manner the customs authorities tried to stop mal-practice of the dishonest importers who used to deprive the country of having real and actual customs duties on the goods imported. 

 20. In the supplementary affidavit given by respondent Nos. 4 and 5 dated 30-1-97 Annexure-2 shows that it was translation of JAAI's Yellow Book/Silver Book given by JETRO, means, Japan External Trade Organization, Official Trade Promotion Agency under the Ministry of International Trade and Industry. In this Annexure the retail price and whole-sale price of different manufactured vehicles have been given. In this Annexure-2 it is further stated that all the prices are shown in this Yellow Book in the unit of 1,000 Yen. It appears to us that the first cover of this booklet is of yellow color and that is why it is popularly know as Yellow Book. In fact, it is a booklet where the manufacturers of different cars and vehicles of Japan have given the manufacturing prices of the imported cars and vehicles which the customs authority has been following since 1993. 

 21. It is submitted by the learned Advocates for the respondents that this Yellow Book is being used and followed since 1989 in respect of imposing duties on imported motor vehicles. Not only in this country, but also in other importing countries prices contained in this book are being followed. From Annexure-A(I) of this supplementary affidavit- in-opposition \ dated 30-1-79 it appears that the respondent No.4, namely, National Board of Revenue, issued a Standing Order on 9th June, 1994 vide Memo No. 1557/94/Cus in respect of imposing duties with regard to the imported re-conditioned cars and this Standing Order refers to section 30 of the Customs Act. From this Annexure-l(l) of the' supplementary affidavit-in-opposition it appears that imposition of duties upon motor vehicles on the basis of this Yellow Book in our country is being followed from 1993 and on 10th June, 1993 the First Standing Order was issued vide Memo No. 1514/93 Cus by NBR for imposing customs duties upon the imported re-conditioned cars after deducting the depreciation value. Then again another Standing Order was issued on 29th January, 1996 vide Memo No. 1653/96/Cus amending the earlier Standing Order dated 9th June, 1994. The rate of depreciation has also been shown in it and it appears that this Standing Order was issued by the National Board of Revenue for imposition of duties upon the imported goods, namely, reconditioned motor vehicles on the basis of the prices as given by the manufacturers from the exporting country. This Standing Order was modified by issuing another Standing Order on 29th1 January, 1996 and a chart has also been given showing as to how the depreciation value will be determined. The depreciation at any rate will not go above 60M. From this Standing Order it shows as to how the prices would be determined on the basis of the price given by the manufacturers and as to how the importers of this country will have to pay the import duties on the value. 

 22. The learned Advocates for the respondents submit that though there is no mentioning of any section of the Customs Act, yet in pursuance of sections 25 and 30 of the Customs Act the National Board of Revenue is competent to issue such Standing Order for fixation of price upon which duty is to be imposed. So, it appears that the respondents had not arbitrarily or suddenly imposed duties upon the re-conditioned vehicles on the basis of this Yellow Book, but this has been followed in our country since 1993. Further, it cannot be said to be arbitrary in view of the fact that this Yellow Book was procured from Japan External Trade Organisation, an Official Trade Promotion Agency under the Ministry of International' Trade and Industry and this is being used since 1993 and in the meantime hundreds of importers had paid their duties on the basis of this Yellow Book and the Government have been realising the duties upon the re-conditioned imported motor vehicles on the basis of this Yellow Book price from the importers. 

 23. In view of the above, the learned Advocates for the respondents submit that this imposition of duty upon the Yellow Book price of the imported re-conditioned cars and vehicles cannot be said to be illegal or arbitrary. It is their case that to fix such a duty on the price of the Yellow Book value is to stop the manipulation of the dishonest businessmen inasmuch as previously it appeared to the Government that the dishonest business people with a view to deprive the country of actual import duties on re-conditioned cars and vehicles used to show lesser prices in the invoices and bills of lading and in this way the Government was deprived of having the actual and real customs duties from the importers of re-conditioned cars and vehicles. It is their further case that only to save the country from being deprived of such huge amount of customs duties the Government has been following the imposed duty on Yellow Book price with reasonable depreciation so that the importers cannot deprive the Government of the usual duties which the dishonest business people did showing lesser value in their invoices and bills of lading. The booklet viz, the Yellow Book was produced before this Court. In that Yellow Book the prices of the cars and vehicles are written both in Japanese language and English language, particularly, the names, code numbers and prices are given in English language. As such, it cannot be said that there is no existence of any book called Yellow Book or that it has no legal existence. The aforesaid Standing Order of the National Board of Revenue relied upon this Yellow Book for the purpose of imposing customs duties upon used cars and vehicles imported from abroad and such Standing Order recognising the Yellow Book is being followed. From Annexure-I (1) of the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition it appears clearly that on 10th June, 1993, first Standing Order was issued with regard to the imposition of duties upon re-conditioned cars and vehicles and subsequently it was amended from time to time. Not only that the National Board of Revenue also has given a guideline in the Standing Order itself as to how and at what per cent the depreciation prices will be determined and allowed and also it shows that under section 30 of the Customs Act when the bill of entry will be produced, the new exchange rate will be applicable for the goods prevailing on that day. 

 24. Further, the Annexure-I of that supplementary affidavit-in-opposition dated 30-1-96 also has given a guideline as regards depreciation and the money exchange rate when the bill of entry will be produced under section 30 of the Act. Since the Board of Revenue issued the Standing Order with respect to imposition of duties upon the used re-conditioned cars and vehicles on the basis of this Yellow Book from 1993 and since it is being used from that day till now and since hundreds of importers had already paid the customs duties on the basis of the Yellow Book value and the Government had already realised the duties from those business people on that basis and since nobody challenged such imposition of duties earlier and since it is being followed in our country, we are of the view that it cannot be said that the imposition of customs duties on the Yellow Book value for the imported re-conditioned cars and vehicles from abroad is illegal and without jurisdiction. In our view, in order to save the country from being deprived of getting legal and usual customs duties on the re-conditioned cars and vehicles from abroad and also in order to protect the interest of the country from the hands of unscrupulous and dishonest businessmen the Government had to take resort to this policy of imposing customs duties on the basis of Yellow Book value. So it cannot be said that such an action of the authorities is illegal and without jurisdiction, rather we hold that this is being done and followed for the greater interest of the country. 

 25. In this connection it may be mentioned that if all the business' people or importers pay the import duties on the basis of Yellow Book, they will not be prejudiced in any manner whatsoever in view of the fact that whatever duties they will pay to the Government will be included in the real price of the goods concerned and when the importers will sell the goods to the customers, they will sell it at the price including the customs duty. As soon as duty of any kind is paid upon the goods it is merged with the price of the goods. So, the importers of the cars will not be prejudiced in any manner whatsoever if they pay the import duties on the basis of Yellow Book value. In several judicial pronouncements including judgment passed in Writ Petition No.4337 of 1996 and Writ Petition No.4336 of 1996, it had been held that importers will have to pay the duties on the price which is prevailing at the time when bill of entry is submitted If, according to the rate of duty imposed by the Government on the date of submission of the bill of entry the importers pay the duties, it will not cause any prejudice to the importers inasmuch as whatever customs duty they are required to pay to the authority, it will be merged with the price of the goods imported. This will, in fact, in our opinion, save the interest of the country from the hand of dishonest business people. We are also of the view that the Standing Orders issued by the National Board of Revenue from time to time are actually reasonable in view of the fact that the same have given the guideline as well as the rates for imposition of import duties on the re-conditioned cars and vehicles with the chart of the depreciation. In the supplementary affidavit dated 30-1-97 Annexure-2 shows that the booklet, namely, JAAI's Yellow Book/Silver Book was obtained by the Federation of Bangladesh Chambers of Commerce and Industry, Federation Bhaban, Motijheel, Dhaka, from JETRO as stated above. This Yellow Book December, 1996 Edition, was sent by JETRO 

 26. Today before delivering judgment Dr. Kamal Hossain has submitted a supplementary affidavit-in-reply on behalf of the petitioner to the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition dated 2-2-97 filed by respondent Nos. 4 and 5. In this supplementary affidavit-in-reply it is again stated that this Yellow Book has got no legal force as it cannot be treated as law in this country. In this supplementary affidavit-in-reply it is stated that this Yellow Book has got on legal force as it cannot be treated as low in this country. In this supplementary affidavit-in-replay it is stated that this translation extract from the Yellow book and silver Book is incorrect and misleading and malafide. It is Slated further that the petitioner contacted the office of the JETRO and one Mr. Kabir of JETRO confirmed the petitioner 'over telephone' that JETRO does not have any expert and they did not translate the Yellow Book into English, but they arrange to translate the same from elsewhere. Mr. Kabir further confirmed the petitioner that JETRO typed the translated pages on their letter head only and supplied the same under the signature of their own people. Mr. Kabir of JETRO further confirmed the petitioner that the translation of Yellow Book is not a complete translation of the Yellow Book and Silver Book, but the same was only a summary of the Yellow Book. From this paragraph 6 of this supplementary affidavit-in-reply it appears that in a sense Mr Kabir of JETRO had confirmed the existence of Yellow Book and Silver Book. Further, Annexure-2 of the supplementary affidavit shows that this book was procured by the Secretary, Federation of Bangladesh Chambers of Commerce and Industry, but the petitioner had confirmed the authenticity of this Yellow Book from one Mr. Kabir of JETRO over telephone, but nothing on paper or anything else. Even then Mr. Kabir also admitted the existence of this Yellow Book. So, we do not find any substance in the allegation as made in this supplementary affidavit-in-reply dated 26-2-97. In view of the submissions made by the learned Advocates and also our discussion as made above we do not find any substance in the contentions of the learned Advocates for the petitioner. 

 27. With regard to Writ Petition No.2035 of 1996 it appears that the customs duty has been imposed upon the Yellow Book value of the re-conditioned vehicles but not upon invoice value of the goods. In this writ petition the order dated 6-6-96 has been challenged by which it has been directed that the duties should be realised upon the Yellow Book value and not upon the invoice value. The learned Advocate Mr Syed Mahrnudul Ahsan, appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submitted that the assessment of customs duty on the basis of Yellow Book is illegal and without jurisdiction. He submitted that the duties upon the re-conditioned motor vehicles ought to have been imposed upon C & F value which is the invoice value. In this case the letter of credit was opened on 22-4-96 and subsequently the vehicles arrived at Chittagong Port. But it appeared that on 12-12-95 the earlier SRO was amended and the customs duty was imposed upon the re-conditioned motor vehicles in pursuance of SRO dated 12-12-95. So, in this case there should not be any doubt about the imposition of customs duty on the basis of the Yellow Book value inasmuch as by the subsequent SRO dated 12-12-95 the cars and vehicles were taken out from the Appendix-2 of the earlier Notification dated 3-1-94. Now, upon his submission as regards the illegality of imposition of duty on the basis of Yellow Book value we need not give any further explanation inasmuch as we have already given our decision above in Writ Petition No.201 of 1996. The instant case is fully covered by the Yellow Book and, as such, our findings above with regard to Yellow Book value are fully applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case and no new explanation is necessary. In the writ petition he has challenged Annexure-D which is the subsequent SRO dated 12-12-95. With regard to this Notification we have given our reasoning’s and findings above and, as such, we do not find anything new in his submissions. For this reason we hold that no illegality was committed by the authority concerned by imposing duties on the basis of Yellow Book value. So, the contentions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner have got no substance. 

 29. This period of 27 years is more than a reasonable period. It is not that the period of six months or one year or two years or five years has passed from the date .of promulgation of Customs Act. This period of 27 years is sufficiently reasonable period during which the authority ought to have framed rules for greater economic interest of the country, but the Government as well as the National Board of Revenue slept over the matter for such a long period without any reason whatsoever. Had there been the relevant Rules for realisation of duties upon import and export of the goods under the Customs Act, country would have been saved from the curse of malpractice of the dishonest businessmen and corrupt officers in the matter of evading duties upon the goods exported and imported. Since there are no specific rules, it has given opportunities to the dishonest people to do corrupt practice and by this corrupt practice they are depriving the country of having its economic interest in the matter of imposition of duties upon the goods which are exported abroad and imported from foreign countries. We do not find any explanation as to why the authorities remained silent over this matter for such an unusually long period. It is reported that in the neighboring country namely, India, relevant rules of Customs Act have already been framed for the import and export of goods. So, it is desirable that the Government and the National Board of Revenue should frame necessary rules for imposition of duties upon the goods which are imported and exported under this Customs Act and if it is not done, the country will suffer more and more so far its economic interest is concerned. 

 30. In Writ Petition No.5722 of 1996 the petitioner has annexed several newspaper cuttings one is the Daily Ittefaq dated 17-11-1996 Annexure-F. the Daily Purbokon, Chittagong dated 17th July, 1996, Annexure-F(l), the Daily Star dated 5-11-96 Annexure-F(2), the Weekly Nastra dated 31 October to 6 November, 1996 Annexure-F (3) and the daily Ittefaq dated 12-11-96 Annexure-F (4). In this Annexure-F (4) the news with the caption 

 31. At the insistence of this Court only two cases on tariff value were disposed of by a Judgment passed 10 Writ Petition NosA337 of 1-96 and 4336 of 1996 on 17-12-96. From the aforesaid newspaper report it appears to us that the Finance Minister made, some indication blaming the Court that because of the interim orders passed by the High Court Division in those writ petitions, country is going to suffer huge financial loss. In this connection it may not be irrelevant to mention that the relevant authorities were in deep sleep for an unusually long period and 'after about 27 years on one fine morning they' suddenly woke up from slumber and discovered that because of several writ petitions the Government is going to incur huge financial loss. But they failed to understand that, for non-framing of Rules, how many hundreds of crores  of money the country had already suffered loss during this long period of 27 years. If the relevant Rules are not framed this Customs Department will remain as unscrupulous businessmen and corrupt officers' paradise. When the petitioners come before this Court and prima facie show some irregularity and illegality, this Court cannot but interfere with those matters. But as soon as a few writ petitions were filed and petitioners obtained favourable release of goods from this Court, the Government as well as National Board of Revenue ought to have come forward for settling the matters by Court immediately. But they remained silent for long.
